title: Why do some sounds give us chills?
subtitle: Music & the brain
subject: sciences
description: Goosebumps, tingles, a racing heart: music can hijack the circuits we use for pleasure and for survival. Here is why.

hero.hook: One note, and the skin rises. Music has just hijacked your survival brain.

blocks.text: About **55 to 70%** of people get chills from music: goosebumps, tingles, a rush of emotion. Researchers call it the **aesthetic chill**, or simply *chills*.
This is not just a figure of speech. Sound waves set off a real chemical storm in the brain, borrowing circuits built for survival and turning them toward beauty.

When a track “lands,” the brain switches on its **reward system**, the network of areas tied to pleasure, the same one that answers to food, sex, and certain drugs. **Brain imaging**, the techniques that show brain activity at work, reveals two stages. First comes **anticipation**, with a flow of **dopamine**, the pleasure neurotransmitter, while you wait for the big moment. Then comes the chill itself, when the pleasure breaks open.

Here is the chemical proof: **naltrexone**, a drug that blocks the **opioid** receptors used by our natural pleasure molecules, can almost erase the pleasure of music. So the brain makes its own internal “drugs” to reward an experience of beauty.
About **5%** of people feel no pleasure at all in music, even with normal hearing. The name for it is **musical anhedonia**, the inability to take pleasure in music.

sections.title: The surprise that raises a chill

blocks.text: A chill often begins with a [[Musical expectation violation]]. The brain is constantly predicting the next note. A choir that comes in too early, a **modulation**, an unexpected change of key, a tension that takes too long to resolve: the emotional alarm lights up.

The **amygdala**, a deep brain region tied to danger, reacts within a fraction of a second. Goosebumps are an old reflex: raise the hair to look bigger or to hold the heat in. Then the cortex works out that this is art, not a threat. The relief turns into intense pleasure.
The proper name for goosebumps is **piloerection**, the raising of body hair. In modern humans, music sets it off mostly during sad or melancholy passages.

sections.title: Why some people are more sensitive

blocks.text: The researcher [[Matthew Sachs]] showed that people prone to chills often have more **white matter**, the fibers that link brain areas, running between the auditory cortex, the prefrontal cortex, and the **insula**, the region that pulls emotions together. Their brain wires sound to feeling more directly.

The trait also travels with [[openness to experience]]: curiosity, and a taste for complexity and ambiguity. The more you welcome the unexpected, the more chances the brain has to fire off its reward.

In Darwinian terms, the musical chill is a paradox: it neither feeds nor protects. But putting the emotions of a group in step may have helped **social cohesion**. The frequencies that hit hardest also recall crying or cries of distress: urgency first, beauty afterward.
At bottom, music hijacks ancient systems to deliver one of the most physical experiences in art: a vibration of the air that becomes a feeling on the skin.
Musical chills come from a release of dopamine triggered by a harmonic surprise, above all in brains strongly wired between hearing and emotion.
